title: The upper room (Mark 14:12–25)
hook: take, this is my body; this is my blood of the covenant

segments.voice: Yesterday, a broken jar of perfume and a bag of silver. Your line was she has done a beautiful thing. What beautiful, impractical thing did you do? Day two hundred nineteen.

It's the day the Passover lambs are sacrificed, and the disciples ask: where do you want us to prepare the meal? Jesus gives instructions that sound like a spy novel. Go into the city. You'll see a man carrying a jar of water. In that world, carrying water was usually women's work, so he'll stand out. Follow him. Wherever he goes in, ask the owner for the guest room, and he'll show you a large upper room, furnished and ready. They find it all just as he said. That evening, the twelve recline at the table with him. And while they're eating, he says it: one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me. And they grow sad, and one by one they ask: "Is it I?"
screen: `FOLLOW THE MAN WITH THE WATER JAR.` → `A LARGE UPPER ROOM.` → `IS IT I?`

segments.voice: Nobody points at anyone else. Each one wonders about himself. And then, still at the table, he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. In the King James Bible: "Take, eat: this is my body." Then he takes a cup, gives thanks, and they all drink from it, and he says: "This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many." That word testament is today's word. In Greek it's diathēkē, and it means covenant: a binding promise that makes two parties belong to each other. It's why the two halves of the Christian Bible are called the Old and New Testaments. The old and new covenants. And listen to the echo. At Mount Sinai, Moses sprinkled blood on the people and called it the blood of the covenant. At a Passover meal, the feast of freedom from Egypt, Jesus takes those words onto his own lips. Then he says he won't drink wine again until he drinks it new in the kingdom of God. Christians have gathered around this meal ever since, and they understand it in different ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians believe the bread and wine truly become his body and blood. Lutherans say he is truly present in, with and under them. Many Reformed Christians speak of a real spiritual presence, and many Baptist and other churches keep it as a memorial. They call it the Eucharist, from the Greek for gave thanks, the Mass, the Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion, the Lord's Supper. The same four verbs in every one: took, blessed, broke, gave.
screen: `IS IT I?` · `TAKE, EAT: THIS IS MY BODY.` · `DIATHEKE: TESTAMENT, COVENANT.` · `ONE MEAL, MANY UNDERSTANDINGS.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BLOOD OF THE NEW TESTAMENT, WHICH IS SHED FOR MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: break bread with thanks. If you have bread, a cracker, anything nearby, hold it. If not, picture the next thing you'll eat. Settle, and breathe. Notice the four verbs: take it, give thanks, break it, share it or eat it. Slowly. Feel it tear. Think of the people who grew it, baked it, carried it. This isn't communion, just a meal, but it can be eaten with thanks. If you pray, you can give thanks to God before you eat. The bell holds the time.
Covenant. In Greek, diathēkē: a binding promise, and the old English word testament. The new covenant, in a cup.
Your line: take, this is my body. Today, at one meal, pause before eating: take, give thanks, break, share. Day two hundred nineteen.

screen: `DAY 219 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: EVEN IF ALL FALL AWAY.`

howItsDone: Christians celebrate this meal as the Eucharist, Mass, Divine Liturgy, Holy Communion or the Lord's Supper, some daily, some weekly, some monthly, repeating Jesus's words over bread and wine; churches differ in how they understand Christ's presence in it.

original.note: Greek: covenant, a binding arrangement; in older English, testament.

trapdoor: what you thought: a last dinner before he died.
what it means: at a Passover meal, Jesus gives bread and cup as his body and his blood of the covenant, and his followers have kept the meal ever since.
what a scholar hears: diathēkē, and the blood of the covenant from Exodus 24:8. the oldest manuscripts of Mark may lack the word new.

notes: Water-carrying as usually women's work: a common commentary note; confirm.
Mark 14:24: 'new' (kainēs) is absent from several early manuscripts (e.g. Sinaiticus, Vaticanus); mentioned only in the trapdoor as 'may lack'. Confirm.

Eucharistic theologies summarized without ranking: Catholic and Orthodox (real change), Lutheran (in, with and under), Reformed (real spiritual presence), Baptist and others (memorial). Keeper to confirm each is fair.
Practice explicitly says it is not communion, to respect churches' sacramental practice. Confirm.
The Synoptic dating of the supper as a Passover meal is followed; John's Gospel dates it differently. Not raised.
